items.text: The first computer bug was real: in 1947 a moth was found in a relay of the Harvard Mark II and taped into the log with the note first actual case of bug being found.
The QWERTY layout appeared in the 1870s on Christopher Sholes typewriters, long before computers.
Ada Lovelace is often called the first programmer: in 1843 she published an algorithm for Charles Babbage analytical engine.
The Python language is named not after the snake, but after the British comedy show Monty Python Flying Circus.
The first website in the world was launched by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1991.
The word robot first appeared in Karel Capek play in 1920; it was coined by his brother, the artist Josef Capek.
The Apollo onboard computer had about two thousand words of RAM.
Software for the Apollo lunar program was built by a team led by Margaret Hamilton. A famous photo shows her next to a stack of printouts as tall as she is.
In 1991 Linus Torvalds announced his operating system as just a hobby. That is how Linux began.
Linus Torvalds wrote the Git version-control system in 2005 in just a few weeks.
The phrase Hello, world became famous thanks to Kernighan and Ritchie book on the C language from 1978.
Unix time counts seconds from midnight on 1 January 1970.
On 19 January 2038 the thirty-two-bit Unix time counter will overflow. This is called the Year 2038 problem.
One of the first electronic computers in continental Europe, MESM, was built in Kyiv under Sergey Lebedev and started working in the early 1950s.
In 1888 stenographer Frank McGurrin won a famous typing contest using all ten fingers blind. After that touch typing quickly became the standard.
The at sign in email addresses was first used by engineer Ray Tomlinson in 1971.
The most frequent letter in English texts is E; in Russian texts it is O.
The brain is about two percent of body mass but uses roughly one fifth of the body energy.
German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve in 1885. Spaced repetition for learning English words is based on it.
Sleep helps lock in what you learned: during sleep the brain moves new knowledge into long-term memory.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach Earth.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object from Earth.
A day on Venus is longer than its year: the planet spins on its axis more slowly than it orbits the Sun.
The International Space Station orbits Earth roughly every ninety minutes, so the crew sees about sixteen sunrises a day.
On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin made the first human flight into space. The flight lasted one hundred and eight minutes.
The first artificial Earth satellite was launched on 4 October 1957.
In zero gravity tears do not run down the cheeks; they gather into a water blob by the eye.
The Moon moves away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres per year.
More than one thousand three hundred Earth-sized planets would fit inside Jupiter.
The transistor, foundation of all modern electronics, was invented at Bell Labs in 1947.
In 1965 Gordon Moore noted that the number of transistors on a chip grows exponentially. That observation became Moore law.
The first computer mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart. Its body was wooden.
One of the first electronic computers, ENIAC, weighed about twenty-seven tonnes and filled an entire hall.
The word bit is short for binary digit. Claude Shannon introduced it into scientific use in 1948.
The eight-bit byte became standard largely thanks to IBM System/360 computers from 1964.
Brendan Eich created the first version of JavaScript in about ten days in 1995.
The first emoji set was drawn by Japanese designer Shigetaka Kurita in 1999. It had one hundred and seventy-six icons.
When reading, the eyes do not move smoothly but in jumps — saccades. We take in text during brief stops between jumps.
The phrase The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog contains every letter of the English alphabet. Such phrases are called pangrams.
A Russian pangram: Eat more of these soft French rolls and drink some tea. It contains every letter of the Russian alphabet.
The word alphabet comes from the names of the first two Greek letters — alpha and beta.
Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic script. The Cyrillic alphabet, named after Cyril, was according to most scholars composed later by their students.
An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
Botanically, a banana is a berry, and a strawberry is not.
Ice floats because water expands when it freezes and becomes lighter.
A lightning channel heats up to several times the temperature of the surface of the Sun.
Looking at a screen, people blink much less than usual. Hence the twenty-twenty-twenty rule: every twenty minutes look for twenty seconds at something about twenty feet away.
The first SMS in the world was sent in 1992. The text was Merry Christmas.
Wikipedia appeared in 2001.
The name Google comes from googol — a one followed by one hundred zeros.
Tetris was invented by Alexey Pajitnov in 1984 at the Computing Centre of the Academy of Sciences in Moscow.
The word pixel is short for picture element.
The first production IBM hard disk from 1956 held about four megabytes and weighed nearly a tonne.
CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.
The F and J keys have small bumps. They help fingers find the home row for touch typing without looking at the keyboard.
The most pressed key when typing ordinary text is the space bar.
In space it is silent: sound needs air or another medium, and in vacuum it has nothing to travel through.
Sunsets on Mars look bluish: Martian dust scatters light differently from Earth air.
Saturn average density is less than that of water. In a giant ocean it would not sink.
Programmer indexes usually start at zero, not one. That makes it easier to compute the offset from the start of an array in memory.
